claim: Mouse Purkinje cells are born at midgestation.
source: We demonstrate that mouse Purkinje cells (PCs), which are born at midgestation and are crucial for development and function of cerebellar circuits, are rapidly and fully regenerated following their ablation at birth.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about PC development.

claim: Mouse Purkinje cells are crucial for development and function of cerebellar circuits.
source: We demonstrate that mouse Purkinje cells (PCs), which are born at midgestation and are crucial for development and function of cerebellar circuits, are rapidly and fully regenerated following their ablation at birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mouse Purkinje cells are rapidly and fully regenerated following their ablation at birth.
source: We demonstrate that mouse Purkinje cells (PCs), which are born at midgestation and are crucial for development and function of cerebellar circuits, are rapidly and fully regenerated following their ablation at birth.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: New PCs are produced from immature FOXP2+ Purkinje cell precursors (iPCs).
source: New PCs are produced from immature FOXP2+ Purkinje cell precursors (iPCs) that are able to enter the cell cycle and support normal cerebellum development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing FOXP2+ cells that are CALB1-/low can proliferate.

claim: Immature FOXP2+ Purkinje cell precursors (iPCs) are able to enter the cell cycle.
source: New PCs are produced from immature FOXP2+ Purkinje cell precursors (iPCs) that are able to enter the cell cycle and support normal cerebellum development.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation experiments and Ki67/pH3 staining showing iPCs can proliferate.

claim: iPCs support normal cerebellum development.
source: New PCs are produced from immature FOXP2+ Purkinje cell precursors (iPCs) that are able to enter the cell cycle and support normal cerebellum development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cerebellum size and function are normal when PCs are regenerated at P1.

claim: The number of iPCs diminishes soon after birth.
source: The number of iPCs and their regenerative capacity, however, diminish soon after birth and consequently PCs are poorly replenished when ablated at postnatal day five.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data showing a decrease in iPC numbers from P1 to P5.

claim: The regenerative capacity of iPCs diminishes soon after birth.
source: The number of iPCs and their regenerative capacity, however, diminish soon after birth and consequently PCs are poorly replenished when ablated at postnatal day five.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data showing reduced proliferation of iPCs at P5 compared to P1.

claim: PCs are poorly replenished when ablated at postnatal day five.
source: The number of iPCs and their regenerative capacity, however, diminish soon after birth and consequently PCs are poorly replenished when ablated at postnatal day five.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data showing persistent reduction in PC numbers at P30 after ablation at P5.

claim: PC-depleted cerebella reach a normal size by increasing cell size when PCs are ablated at P5.
source: Nevertheless, the PC-depleted cerebella reach a normal size by increasing cell size, but scaling of neuron types is disrupted and cerebellar function is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by measurements showing normal cerebellar area at P30 despite reduced PC numbers, and increased PC soma size and dendrite length.

claim: Scaling of neuron types is disrupted in PC-depleted cerebella when PCs are ablated at P5.
source: Nevertheless, the PC-depleted cerebella reach a normal size by increasing cell size, but scaling of neuron types is disrupted and cerebellar function is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by data showing altered ratios of PCs to granule cells in P5-PC-DTR animals.

claim: Cerebellar function is impaired when PCs are ablated at P5.
source: Nevertheless, the PC-depleted cerebella reach a normal size by increasing cell size, but scaling of neuron types is disrupted and cerebellar function is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing showing motor deficits in P5-PC-DTR mice.

claim: Most neurons in the brain are generated at specific developmental time points.
source: Most neurons in the brain are generated at specific developmental time points, and once a neuron becomes postmitotic regeneration following injury is limited, except for in two forebrain regions that maintain neurogenesis (Chaker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Once a neuron becomes postmitotic regeneration following injury is limited, except for in two forebrain regions that maintain neurogenesis.
source: Most neurons in the brain are generated at specific developmental time points, and once a neuron becomes postmitotic regeneration following injury is limited, except for in two forebrain regions that maintain neurogenesis (Chaker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Adult forebrain neurons undergo limited recovery following injury that involves either reactive gliosis or migration of neural stem cells from the neurogenic niches.
source: In the context of injury, adult forebrain neurons undergo limited recovery that involves either reactive gliosis (Buffo et al., 2008; Robel et al., 2011; Sirko et al., 2013) or migration of neural stem cells from the neurogenic niches (Benner et al., 2013; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015; López-Juárez et al., 2013; Martí-Fàbregas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The cerebellum of the hindbrain has a complex folded structure that houses the majority of neurons in the brain.
source: The cerebellum (CB) of the hindbrain has a complex folded structure that houses the majority of neurons in the brain and is essential for balance and motor coordination, as well as higher order reasoning via circuits it forms throughout the forebrain (Fatemi et al., 2012; Steinlin, 2007; Tavano et al., 2007; Tsai et al., 2012; Wagner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The cerebellum is essential for balance and motor coordination, as well as higher order reasoning via circuits it forms throughout the forebrain.
source: The cerebellum (CB) of the hindbrain has a complex folded structure that houses the majority of neurons in the brain and is essential for balance and motor coordination, as well as higher order reasoning via circuits it forms throughout the forebrain (Fatemi et al., 2012; Steinlin, 2007; Tavano et al., 2007; Tsai et al., 2012; Wagner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: For two weeks after birth, the postnatal mouse CB consists of both neurons generated in the embryo, and two neurogenic progenitor pools that produce late born neurons and glia.
source: For two weeks after birth, the postnatal mouse CB consists of both neurons generated in the embryo, and two neurogenic progenitor pools that produce late born neurons and glia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: The proliferating granule cell progenitors can be replenished following injury by adaptive reprograming of the second Nestin-expressing progenitors.
source: Interestingly, the proliferating granule cell progenitors can be replenished following injury by adaptive reprograming of the second Nestin-expressing progenitors (Wojcinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding and supported by a citation.

claim: Purkinje cells are born by embryonic day (E) 13.5 in the mouse.
source: Purkinje cells (PC) are born by embryonic day (E) 13.5 in the mouse and during weeks 10–11 in humans (Rakic and Sidman, 1970; Wang and Zoghbi, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Purkinje cells are born during weeks 10–11 in humans.
source: Purkinje cells (PC) are born by embryonic day (E) 13.5 in the mouse and during weeks 10–11 in humans (Rakic and Sidman, 1970; Wang and Zoghbi, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: After exiting the cell cycle in the ventricular zone, PCs express FOXP2 as they migrate to form a PC layer (PCL) under the cerebellar surface by E17.5.
source: After exiting the cell cycle in the ventricular zone, PCs express FOXP2 as they migrate to form a PC layer (PCL) under the cerebellar surface by E17.5, and turn on Calbindin1 (CALB1) in the late embryo and stop expressing FOXP2 by two weeks after birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PC development.

claim: PCs turn on Calbindin1 (CALB1) in the late embryo.
source: After exiting the cell cycle in the ventricular zone, PCs express FOXP2 as they migrate to form a PC layer (PCL) under the cerebellar surface by E17.5, and turn on Calbindin1 (CALB1) in the late embryo and stop expressing FOXP2 by two weeks after birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PC development.

claim: PCs stop expressing FOXP2 by two weeks after birth.
source: After exiting the cell cycle in the ventricular zone, PCs express FOXP2 as they migrate to form a PC layer (PCL) under the cerebellar surface by E17.5, and turn on Calbindin1 (CALB1) in the late embryo and stop expressing FOXP2 by two weeks after birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PC development.

claim: PCs play a central role in postnatal CB development by being the main source of sonic hedgehog (SHH).
source: PCs play a central role in postnatal CB development by being the main source of sonic hedgehog (SHH), which is required for proliferation of granule cell progenitors and Nestin-expressing progenitors that produce interneurons and astrocytes (Corrales et al., 2006; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is required for proliferation of granule cell progenitors and Nestin-expressing progenitors that produce interneurons and astrocytes.
source: PCs play a central role in postnatal CB development by being the main source of sonic hedgehog (SHH), which is required for proliferation of granule cell progenitors and Nestin-expressing progenitors that produce interneurons and astrocytes (Corrales et al., 2006; Fleming et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: PCs are key for CB function by integrating the inputs that converge on the cerebellar cortex.
source: PCs also are key for CB function by integrating the inputs that converge on the cerebellar cortex (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: PC loss is linked to cerebellar motor behavior syndromes.
source: Hence, PC loss is linked to cerebellar motor behavior syndromes and has also been implicated in autism (Fatemi et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: PC loss has been implicated in autism.
source: Hence, PC loss is linked to cerebellar motor behavior syndromes and has also been implicated in autism (Fatemi et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Only 52.16 ± 21.84% of PCs expressed TdT and DTR at postnatal day (P) 1 in PC-DTR mice.
source: We found that only 52.16 ± 21.84% of PCs (n = 5 mice), identified by expression of CALB1, expressed TdT and DTR at postnatal day (P) 1, and surprisingly the percentage and large variation remained similar at P5 and P30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of PCs expressing TdT and DTR and the large variation remained similar at P5 and P30 in PC-DTR mice.
source: We found that only 52.16 ± 21.84% of PCs (n = 5 mice), identified by expression of CALB1, expressed TdT and DTR at postnatal day (P) 1, and surprisingly the percentage and large variation remained similar at P5 and P30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When DT was injected at P1 into PC-DTR pups, nearly all TdT+ PCs formed an ectopic layer below the PC layer (PCL) by 1 day post injection (dpi).
source: Strikingly, when DT was injected at P1 into PC-DTR pups (P1-PC-DTR), nearly all TdT+ PCs formed an ectopic layer below the PC layer (PCL) by 1 day post injection (dpi) (Figure 1A–M).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ectopic layer was absent by P8 in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: The ectopic layer was absent by P8 (Figure 1K), and TdT+ cells in the ectopic layer were TUNEL positive starting at P3 with a peak at P5.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: TdT+ cells in the ectopic layer were TUNEL positive starting at P3 with a peak at P5 in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: The ectopic layer was absent by P8 (Figure 1K), and TdT+ cells in the ectopic layer were TUNEL positive starting at P3 with a peak at P5.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data showing apoptosis of TdT+ cells.

claim: Almost all DTR-expressing TdT+ cells become misplaced, die and are cleared within 5–7 dpi of DT in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: These results show that almost all DTR-expressing TdT+ cells become misplaced, die and are cleared within 5–7 dpi of DT (Figure 1N,O).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The number of CALB1+ PCs in the PCL of P1-PC-DTR mice was significantly reduced at P2 compared to non-injected controls.
source: Unexpectedly, although the number of CALB1+ PCs in the PCL of P1-PC-DTR mice was significantly reduced at P2 compared to non-injected controls (No DT), it was not significantly reduced at P3 and later stages (Figure 1P).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The number of CALB1+ PCs in the PCL of P1-PC-DTR mice was not significantly reduced at P3 and later stages compared to non-injected controls.
source: Unexpectedly, although the number of CALB1+ PCs in the PCL of P1-PC-DTR mice was significantly reduced at P2 compared to non-injected controls (No DT), it was not significantly reduced at P3 and later stages (Figure 1P).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The total number of PCs (ectopic layer + PCL) was significantly greater in DT-injected cerebella than in No DT controls at P2 and P3.
source: Furthermore, the total number of PCs (ectopic layer + PCL) was significantly greater in DT-injected cerebella than in No DT controls at P2 and P3, and the total number of PCs was down to normal levels at P5, overlapping with the time of clearance of the ectopic layer (Figure 1P).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The total number of PCs was down to normal levels at P5 in P1-PC-DTR mice, overlapping with the time of clearance of the ectopic layer.
source: Furthermore, the total number of PCs (ectopic layer + PCL) was significantly greater in DT-injected cerebella than in No DT controls at P2 and P3, and the total number of PCs was down to normal levels at P5, overlapping with the time of clearance of the ectopic layer (Figure 1P).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The number of TdT+ cells in the PCL increased between P8 and P30 in P1-PC-DTR brains.
source: Although the number of TdT+ cells in the PCL increased between P8 and P30 in P1-PC-DTR brains, it remained significantly lower than in No DT controls at P30 (Figure 1Q).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The number of TdT+ cells in the PCL remained significantly lower than in No DT controls at P30 in P1-PC-DTR brains.
source: Although the number of TdT+ cells in the PCL increased between P8 and P30 in P1-PC-DTR brains, it remained significantly lower than in No DT controls at P30 (Figure 1Q).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: There is no significant increase in the recombination induced by Pcp2Cre after birth in the control postnatal CB.
source: Given that there is no significant increase in the recombination induced by Pcp2Cre after birth in the control postnatal CB (Figure 1Q, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), the percentage of TdT+ cells in P1-PC-DTR brains at P30 (~25–30%) matched the predicted percentage if 50% of the PCs were killed by DT and then ~50% of the regenerated PCs underwent recombination.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1Q and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The percentage of TdT+ cells in P1-PC-DTR brains at P30 (~25–30%) matched the predicted percentage if 50% of the PCs were killed by DT and then ~50% of the regenerated PCs underwent recombination.
source: Given that there is no significant increase in the recombination induced by Pcp2Cre after birth in the control postnatal CB (Figure 1Q, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), the percentage of TdT+ cells in P1-PC-DTR brains at P30 (~25–30%) matched the predicted percentage if 50% of the PCs were killed by DT and then ~50% of the regenerated PCs underwent recombination.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data and recombination efficiency.

claim: No significant decrease in the sectional area of the CB was observed between P1.5 and P30 in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: Interestingly, and consistent with the rapid recovery of PC numbers in the PCL, no significant decrease in the sectional area of the CB was observed between P1.5 and P30 (Figure 1R–T, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1R–T and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The thickness of the outer (proliferating) and inner (differentiating) external granule cell layers remained normal in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: Furthermore, the thickness of the outer (proliferating) and inner (differentiating) external granule cell layers remained normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CB can rapidly recover (within 24–48 hr) from the loss of ~50% of PCs at P1, by producing new PCs and resuming normal growth.
source: In summary, we uncovered that the CB can rapidly recover (within 24–48 hr) from the loss of ~50% of PCs at P1, by producing new PCs and resuming normal growth.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: BrdU+ PCs (FoxP2+ and CALB1+) were observed in the PCL of all groups of P1-PC-DTR mice given BrdU at different time points after DT injection.
source: P1-PC-DTR mice were divided into four groups; each group receiving three injections of BrdU (2 hr apart) during 4–26 hr after DT-injection (Figure 2A). As predicted, BrdU+ PCs (FoxP2+ and CALB1+) were observed in the PCL of all groups (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with the greatest incorporation being between 10–20 hr after DT (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greatest BrdU incorporation in PCs was between 10–20 hr after DT in P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: P1-PC-DTR mice were divided into four groups; each group receiving three injections of BrdU (2 hr apart) during 4–26 hr after DT-injection (Figure 2A). As predicted, BrdU+ PCs (FoxP2+ and CALB1+) were observed in the PCL of all groups (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with the greatest incorporation being between 10–20 hr after DT (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In No DT mice no incorporation of BrdU was observed in PCs.
source: Importantly, in No DT mice no incorporation of BrdU was observed in PCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: FOXP2 and BrdU showed non-overlapping subnuclear localization in the nuclei of PCs.
source: Curiously, FOXP2 and BrdU showed non-overlapping subnuclear localization in the nuclei of PCs.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: BrdU+ mature PCs with similar cell bodies and dendritic trees to their neighbors were observed at P30 in P1-PC-DTR mice that had received BrdU 10–14 hr after DT injection.
source: In addition, when we analyzed brains of P1-PC-DTR mice at P30 that had received BrdU 10–14 hr after DT injection, we observed BrdU+ mature PCs with similar cell bodies and dendritic trees to their neighbors, showing that the newly generated PCs differentiate and survive to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The newly generated PCs differentiate and survive to adulthood.
source: In addition, when we analyzed brains of P1-PC-DTR mice at P30 that had received BrdU 10–14 hr after DT injection, we observed BrdU+ mature PCs with similar cell bodies and dendritic trees to their neighbors, showing that the newly generated PCs differentiate and survive to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of BrdU+ mature PCs at P30.

claim: A lack of BrdU incorporation in the ectopic layer at P3 shows that the labeling of PCs is not due to DNA damage induced by DT-mediated cell death.
source: Furthermore, a lack of BrdU incorporation in the ectopic layer at P3 shows that the labeling of PCs is not due to DNA damage induced by DT-mediated cell death (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In irradiated pups, extensive γ-H2AX foci were observed, including in PCs, but BrdU incorporation was not detected in any PCs.
source: In the irradiated pups we observed extensive γ-H2AX foci, including in PCs, but BrdU incorporation was not detected in any PCs.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing irradiation to DT treatment.

claim: P1-PC-DTR mice injected with DT showed BrdU incorporation in PCs without any γ-H2AX foci.
source: In contrast, P1-PC-DTR mice injected with DT showed BrdU incorporation in PCs without any γ-H2AX foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: DNA damage does not account for the BrdU incorporation into PCs following ablation of ~50% of PCs at P1.
source: Thus, DNA damage does not account for the BrdU incorporation into PCs following ablation of ~50% of PCs at P1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of irradiation and DT treatment experiments.

claim: Rare GFP-labeled CALB1+ PCs were observed in P1-PC-DTR animals near the site of injection at P21.
source: When the mice were analyzed at P21, we indeed observed rare GFP-labeled CALB1+ PCs in P1-PC-DTR animals near the site of injection, and not in No DT controls.
evidence: This is an observation from retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: No GFP-labeled CALB1+ PCs were observed in No DT controls at P21.
source: When the mice were analyzed at P21, we indeed observed rare GFP-labeled CALB1+ PCs in P1-PC-DTR animals near the site of injection, and not in No DT controls.
evidence: This is an observation from retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: GFP+ granule cells and Bergmann glia were observed in both the No DT and P1-PC-DTR mice.
source: As expected, GFP+ granule cells and Bergmann glia were observed in both the No DT and P1-PC-DTR mice (Figure 2E–I).
evidence: This is an observation from retroviral labeling experiments shown in Figure 2E–I.

claim: A progenitor capable of proliferating produces the new PCs after ablation at P1.
source: These three sets of experiments thus reveal that a progenitor capable of proliferating produces the new PCs after ablation at P1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BrdU, EdU, and retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: No CFP+ cells were found to co-express FOXP2 or CALB1 at 12 hr and 2 days post DT injection in P1-PC-DTR mice and in No DT controls using a Nes-CFP reporter allele.
source: However, when we tested the contribution of NEPs to PC regeneration using a Nes-CFP reporter allele that transiently maintains CFP protein after differentiation, no CFP+ cells were found to co-express FOXP2 or CALB1 at 12 hr and 2 days post DT injection in P1-PC-DTR mice and in No DT controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inducible fate mapping of NEPs using Nestin-FlpoER/+; R26FSF-TdT/+ mice showed no TdT+ PCs at P30 in P1-PC-DTR and No DT control mice given tamoxifen at P0.
source: Furthermore, inducible fate mapping of NEPs using Nestin-FlpoER/+; R26FSF-TdT/+ (FSF = frt stop-frt) mice showed no TdT+ PCs at P30 in P1-PC-DTR and No DT control mice given tamoxifen at P0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: A progenitor other than NEPs mediates regeneration following PC depletion.
source: These results suggest that a progenitor other than NEPs mediates regeneration following PC depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Nestin reporter and fate mapping experiments.

claim: At P1, CALB1 negative/low and FOXP2-expressing cells (iPCs) were identified.
source: We next examined whether a progenitor exists after birth that expresses early (FOXP2) but not late (CALB1) PC markers. Indeed, at P1 we identified CALB1 negative/low and FOXP2-expressing cells that could be immature PCs (named iPC for immature Purkinje cells; Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: iPCs were not labeled by Pcp2Cre as they were TdT and DTR negative in No DT controls, thus they escape DT-mediated cell death.
source: Possibly accounting for the regeneration of PCs, iPCs were not labeled by Pcp2Cre as they were TdT and DTR negative in No DT controls, thus they escape DT-mediated cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of iPCs decreased from P1 (74.33 ± 5.69/midline sagittal section) to P5 (28.66 ± 7.51/midline sagittal section).
source: Temporal analyses revealed a decrease in the number of iPCs from P1 (74.33 ± 5.69/midline sagittal section) to P5 (28.66 ± 7.51/midline sagittal section, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating the progenitors are a transient population.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: iPCs are a transient population.
source: Temporal analyses revealed a decrease in the number of iPCs from P1 (74.33 ± 5.69/midline sagittal section) to P5 (28.66 ± 7.51/midline sagittal section, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating the progenitors are a transient population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of decreasing iPC numbers over time.

claim: The few iPCs present at P5 were specifically enriched in the central and nodular zones of the CB, which are developmentally delayed at P5.
source: Interestingly, the few iPCs present at P5 were specifically enriched in the central and nodular zones of the CB, which are developmentally delayed at P5 (Legué et al., 2015; Sudarov and Joyner, 2007)(Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and supported by citations.

claim: A significant reduction in the number of iPCs was observed between P1 and P5 in C57BL/6 inbred strain of mice.
source: In order to investigate the normal fate of iPCs, we tested whether there is an increase in the number of CALB1+ PCs from P1 to P30. In order to minimize variation across animals, we used the C57BL/6 inbred strain of mice and analyzed the entire half-vermis of each brain (every second section). As expected, a significant reduction in the number of iPCs was observed between P1 and P5, but in addition we detected a significant increase in the number of CALB1+ cells at P30 compared to P1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant increase in the number of CALB1+ cells at P30 compared to P1 was detected in C57BL/6 inbred strain of mice.
source: In order to investigate the normal fate of iPCs, we tested whether there is an increase in the number of CALB1+ PCs from P1 to P30. In order to minimize variation across animals, we used the C57BL/6 inbred strain of mice and analyzed the entire half-vermis of each brain (every second section). As expected, a significant reduction in the number of iPCs was observed between P1 and P5, but in addition we detected a significant increase in the number of CALB1+ cells at P30 compared to P1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At P5 there was a trend towards an increase in the number of CALB1+ cells.
source: At P5 there was a trend towards an increase in the number of CALB1+ cells.
evidence: This is an observation from quantitative data analysis.

claim: There was a trend towards a reduction in the total number of iPCs plus CALB1+ cells at P5 and P30 compared to P1.
source: There was also a trend towards a reduction in the total number of iPCs plus CALB1+ cells at P5 and P30 compared to P1 (Figure 3C), suggesting that some PCs may also undergo apoptosis during early postnatal development.
evidence: This is an observation from quantitative data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Some PCs may undergo apoptosis during early postnatal development.
source: There was also a trend towards a reduction in the total number of iPCs plus CALB1+ cells at P5 and P30 compared to P1 (Figure 3C), suggesting that some PCs may also undergo apoptosis during early postnatal development.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the trend towards reduction in total PC numbers.

claim: iPCs are cells destined to become PCs, but normally undergo a delay in differentiation until the first week after birth.
source: These results provide evidence that iPCs are cells destined to become PCs, but normally undergo a delay in differentiation until the first week after birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of increasing CALB1+ cells and decreasing iPCs over time.

claim: The number of iPCs showed a significant increase 12 hr after DT injection in P1-PC-DTR mice (1.90 ± 0.05 fold).
source: Quantification of iPC numbers showed a significant increase 12 hr after DT injection in P1-PC-DTR mice (1.90 ± 0.05 fold, Figure 3D), correlating with the time window of highest BrdU incorporation after injury (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At P5 the number of iPCs was significantly lower in P1-PC-DTR animals than in No DT mice.
source: Interestingly, at P5 the number of iPCs was significantly lower in P1-PC-DTR animals than in No DT mice (Figure 3D), possibly reflecting an exhaustion of the progenitor population by production of new PCs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduction in iPCs at P5 in P1-PC-DTR animals possibly reflects an exhaustion of the progenitor population by production of new PCs.
source: Interestingly, at P5 the number of iPCs was significantly lower in P1-PC-DTR animals than in No DT mice (Figure 3D), possibly reflecting an exhaustion of the progenitor population by production of new PCs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of reduced iPCs at P5.

claim: All CALB1+ PCs and iPCs expressed TdT at P1 in FoxP2Flpo/+; R26FSF-TdT/+ mice.
